newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: No word on Fokker as deadline looms.
newsitem.headline: No word on Fokker as deadline looms.

text.p: As an end-of-month deadline loomed Thursday there was still no word on whether South Korea's Samsung Aerospace and the Dutch state were any closer to a deal to relaunch bankrupt Dutch plane maker Fokker.

Court-appointed administrators who have been running Fokker since it was declared bankrupt in March gave Samsung the exclusive right to examine Fokker's books in September with a view to a possible bid for its core plane-making business.

Samsung sees a resurrected Fokker as a potential shortcut to fulfilling its ambition of becoming a major player in the global aerospace industry. But it is unwilling to assume all the risks and has sought substantial investment by the Dutch government.

The government has indicated it is willing to provide fresh capital for a new Fokker and invest in the development of a new 125-seat regional jet, but Samsung is said to have baulked at its demands for long-term job guarantees in the Netherlands.

Since March the administrators have kept Fokker running with a skeleton staff of 650 people, working on the assumption that a relaunch of the company would provide the best deal for Fokker's creditors, its employees and the Dutch economy.
But with suppliers increasingly anxious about Fokker's ability to pay its bills, the administrators have said the talks with Samsung must be completed by the end of October.
If those talks fail to bear fruit, one of the world's oldest aviation companies seems headed for an undignified ending: a piecemeal sale of its remaining assets to the highest bidder.
Most of the companies who showed an interest in Fokker in the early days of the bankruptcy, such as Canada's Bombardier, have long since disappeared from the scene.
Russia's Yakovlev says it remains interested, but is not regarded in the Netherlands as a serious partner for Fokker.
Many of the other players in the overcrowded and fiercely competitive regional jet market would probably be glad to see the administrators bang the last nail into Fokker's coffin.

Fokker, founded in 1919 by Dutch aviation pioneer Anthony Fokker, is one of the oldest names in the industry and its F27 Friendship turboprop, launched in 1957, was one of the industry's biggest commercial successes.
But in more recent years Fokker struggled to achieve financial stability and swapped industry partners several times.
In 1993 Daimler Benz Aerospace paid 686 million guilders ($404.6 million) for a 51 percent stake in Fokker.

But despite job cuts and tight cost controls, depressed world aircraft markets and a weak dollar saw the company steadily lose altitude and sink into deeper and deeper losses that had to be met by DASA and the Dutch government.
In January 1996, Daimler said it could no longer bear Fokker's huge losses and cut off financial support, forcing the company into bankruptcy two months later.
